**On the Word "Meanwhile"**

There's a word I've grown fond of, and it's not a glamorous one. It doesn't have the rolling music of *serendipity* or the smoky mystery of *penumbra*. It's a connective, a bit of narrative plumbing, the kind of word that gets you from one scene to the next without anyone noticing the joinery. The word is *meanwhile*, and I think it might be one of the most quietly radical words in the language.

Consider what it does. A story is moving along—someone is walking through a market, say, arguing with a fishmonger about the price of mackerel—and then the narrator says *meanwhile*, and suddenly we're somewhere else entirely. A ship is taking on water three hundred miles offshore. A child is learning to whistle. A woman in a city the fishmonger will never visit is deciding, at this exact moment, to leave her husband. The word insists that all of it is happening at once, that the mackerel argument does not pause for the shipwreck, that the whistle and the departure share a second.

We know this, of course. We know the world is simultaneous. But we don't *feel* it most of the time, because attention is a narrow beam and consciousness is stubbornly serial. I can only be in one room. I can only follow one thread of thought at a time, and even that with difficulty. The default texture of experience is *and then, and then, and then*—a single lane, one thing after another. *Meanwhile* is the word that cuts a window in the wall of that lane and shows you the traffic on the other side.

Old stories didn't always have it. Or rather, they had it, but they used it sparingly, because the technology of the narrative eye was still developing. Epic poetry tends to follow its hero; when it leaves him, it leaves him for the gods, who are permitted to see everything because that's their job. It took a long time for ordinary human narrators to claim that privilege—to say, in effect, *I will now show you two places at once, and you will hold them both in your mind*. The nineteenth-century novel, with its sprawling casts and its cities full of strangers whose lives intersect by accident, is in some sense a monument to *meanwhile*. Dickens is practically built out of it. So is the newspaper, that daily bundle of unrelated simultaneities: a flood here, an election there, a recipe, an obituary, a baseball score—all of them true on the same date.

What I love about the word is its refusal to rank. *Meanwhile* doesn't say that the shipwreck matters more than the whistling child, or that the leaving wife is the real story and the mackerel is filler. It just says: also this. It's a democratic little word. It grants existence to the background without demanding that the background justify itself. There's something almost tender in that. Most of us spend most of our lives in someone else's meanwhile—the unnamed figure at the next table, the car passing in the rain, the light in a window seen from a train. We are the connective tissue of other people's plots. And the word acknowledges us. It says the plot was never the only thing going on.

I sometimes think the feeling that *meanwhile* names—the vertigo of simultaneity—is one of the core aesthetic experiences available to a person, and one we tend to stumble into rather than seek out. You're standing at a kitchen sink at night and it occurs to you that it is morning somewhere, that people are eating breakfast, that a wedding is ending and a shift is beginning and a fox is crossing a road in a country whose name you'd have to look up. The dishes don't get cleaner. Nothing changes. But for a moment the walls of the single lane go thin, and you feel the size of the thing you're part of. It's not a religious feeling exactly, though it borders on one. It's more like the feeling of realizing the map is much bigger than the part you've been looking at, and that the rest of it isn't blank.

There's a gentler version, too, and it's the one I keep returning to. When someone you love is far away and you don't know what they're doing, *meanwhile* is the word that holds them. You don't have the scene; you just have the knowledge that a scene exists. They are somewhere, doing something, at this very instant, and their instant and yours are the same instant even though you can't see each other. It's a small consolation and a strange one, and I suspect it's part of why people look at the moon when they miss each other: it's the one thing in both frames at once. The moon is the physical form of *meanwhile*.

I don't want to overload the word. It's a humble thing and it should be allowed to stay humble. Most of the time it just gets a paragraph from A to B, and that's fine. But I've come to think that the best words are often the ones that do their real work under cover of doing something ordinary. *Meanwhile* pretends to be about transitions. What it's actually about is the fact that you are never the only story, that the world does not wait, that at this very moment—this one, as you reach the end of this sentence—someone is laughing at a joke you'll never hear, and a kettle is coming to a boil in a kitchen you'll never see, and the fox has made it across the road.

And none of that is a digression. It's the rest of the page.
